title: Quantized onboarding regression — slice casebook
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note documents a compact, slice-focused regression analysis run during model onboarding for quantized variants. The aim is to identify the kinds of prompts and tasks where low-precision builds (AWQ, GPTQ, int8, int4) exhibit meaningful quality deltas vs the fp16 baseline, and to recommend per-slice deployment policies and gating thresholds for Redwood’s onboarding flow.

Executive summary (top-line):
- We ran the onboarding prompt set (1.2k prompts, mixed tasks) across fp16 reference and four quantized variants: AWQ-8, GPTQ-8, int8-dynamic, int4-static.
- Introduced three composite metrics to capture production relevance: Semantic Perturbation Score (SPS), Prompt Robustness Index (PRI), and Hallucination Drift Rate (HDR).
- High-level finding: AWQ-8 preserves SPS best overall (median delta -1.6 pts), GPTQ-8 shows slightly higher variance (median delta -2.4 pts) but better tail on long-context QA, int8-dynamic has modest degradation on factual retrieval slices, and int4-static fails for ~7% of prompts (large HDR).
- Recommendation: enable AWQ by default for hosted API with per-route fallback to fp16 for the small set of hallucination-sensitive slices; gate int4 static to internal-only experiments until we have slice-specific quant-aware prompt tuning.

New slice taxonomy (why different):
We used a different slicing approach than prior audits to better reflect production failure modes. Each prompt was tagged along three orthogonal axes (labels applied by the onboarding prompt set pipeline):
- Intent type: short-answer-fact, long-form-explain, instruction-following, code-completion, multi-turn-chat
- Sensitivity: hallucination-sensitive (needs external facts/IDs), safety-sensitive (toxicity risk), low-risk
- Context length bucket: short (<64 tokens), mid (64–512), long (>512)
This yields interpretable slices like: "short-answer-hallucination-sensitive", "long-form-low-risk", "multi-turn-chat-mid-length".

Metrics (definitions used here):
- Semantic Perturbation Score (SPS): 0–100 scale derived from entailment + embedding similarity + normalized token overlap; lower is worse. We report delta = quantized minus fp16.
- Prompt Robustness Index (PRI): percentage of runs where the top-3 completions overlap by >=0.7 cosine and operator acceptability; captures stability to sampling and numeric instability.
- Hallucination Drift Rate (HDR): fraction of responses with unsupported factual claims relative to a small knowledge oracle (wiki-snapshot) — flagged by our internal hallucination detector.
- Latency and token-cost deltas included but considered secondary for this doc.

Methodology (concise):
- Prompt set: 1,200 prompts selected from onboarding pool (balanced by product route and historical failure log).
- Runs: 5 seeds per prompt with sampling settings matching production (temperature 0.2–0.7 depending on route), deterministic evaluation for QA slices where applicable.
- Post-process: automatic metrics + 300 human spot checks (stratified across slices).
- Hardware: A100 fp16 baseline; quantized models executed on testbench nodes with kernels closest to production environment.

Detailed per-slice notes (selected slices with notable deltas):
1) short-answer-hallucination-sensitive
   - SPS delta: AWQ-8 -2.1, GPTQ-8 -3.0, int8 -4.5, int4 -12.8
   - PRI delta: AWQ -3%, GPTQ -6%, int8 -8%, int4 -28%
   - HDR: AWQ +1.8ppt, GPTQ +3.4ppt, int8 +5.9ppt, int4 +19.2ppt
   - Interpretation: int4 shows catastrophic factual drift here. AWQ acceptable for exploratory routes but for billing/ID returns require fp16 fallback.

2) multi-turn-chat-mid-length
   - SPS delta: AWQ -0.9, GPTQ -1.8, int8 -2.2, int4 -6.7
   - PRI delta: AWQ -1%, GPTQ -3%, int8 -4%, int4 -14%
   - Human notes: GPTQ exhibits slightly better conversational consistency on turn coherency for >6 turns, likely due to KV-cache difference.

3) code-completion-short
   - SPS delta: AWQ -0.6, GPTQ -0.4, int8 -1.1, int4 -4.2
   - PRI delta: AWQ -0.5%, GPTQ -0.3%, int8 -2%, int4 -9%
   - Key note: GPTQ produced slightly fewer parse errors in Python snippets; int4 often truncates or drops closing tokens.

4) long-form-explain-low-risk
   - SPS delta: AWQ -1.2, GPTQ -2.9, int8 -3.4, int4 -8.0
   - HDR: all low (<1%); quality impact is stylistic/fluency rather than hallucination. AWQ preserves coherency best.

5) short-instruction-following (token-light)
   - SPS delta: AWQ -0.2, GPTQ -0.6, int8 -0.9, int4 -3.3
   - Recommendation: safe to enable AWQ and int8 for these unless PRI threshold matters for downstream code.

Aggregate observations (why these patterns might happen):
- AWQ tends to maintain semantic footprint because it adapts quant scales per-weight group and preserves important dynamic ranges that matter for factual assertions.
- GPTQ can produce lower average SPS but sometimes better tail behavior for sequence consistency due to the way KV-cache and layer quantization interact with long contexts on our runtime.
- int4 static quant loses dynamic range causing token-level distortions in rare token classes (numbers, punctuation, identifiers) — explains hallucination spikes in fact-heavy slices.
- int8-dynamic sits in the middle; it is cost-effective and often acceptable for low-sensitivity routes.

Operational recommendations (concrete):
- Default rollout: AWQ-8 for public hosted API with the following per-route policies:
  * Billing/IDs/factual-return routes: force fp16 or implement a fast fp16 fallback when HDR > 2.0ppt for the slice.
  * Chat exploratory routes: AWQ-8 by default; monitor PRI and HDR in the first 48h.
- Int8-dynamic: enable for non-hallucination-sensitive workloads and internal dedicated clusters; set alert if SPS delta < -3 or HDR delta > +4ppt.
- Int4-static: restrict to internal A/B experiments and apply automatic disable if failing >5% of prompts in a route or HDR > +10ppt.
- CI gating: require SPS delta per-slice >= -3.0 AND HDR delta <= +3.0ppt for automatic onboarding approval. If either condition fails, the model is blocked and a remediation ticket is created.

Monitoring and telemetry suggestions:
- Add slice-specific dashboards with SPS, PRI, HDR, and a small human-check sampling track. Alert when any slice crosses gating thresholds.
- Instrument model routing with an A/B fallback counter: record how often quantized variant falls back to fp16 and the user-visible latency delta.

Follow-ups and open questions:
- Investigate why GPTQ sometimes outperforms AWQ on long-form chat tails — hypothesize implementation differences in attention kernel alignment; create a benchmarking ticket to reproduce with isolated kernels (JIRA-ML-1987).
- For int4: test prompt-adaptive quant-aware fine-tuning on hallucination-sensitive slice (pilot n=200 prompts) and report if HDR reduces below +5ppt.
- Expand human spot-checks for low-frequency tokens (IDs, dates) to better characterize numeric token degradation.

Appendix (short):
- Raw aggregate numbers and per-prompt CSV attached in the linked GitHub PR.
- Human check rubric used: acceptability (binary), hallucination flag (binary), severity (0–3).

Conclusion:
This casebook shows AWQ as the best candidate for broad rollout with clear slice-level exceptions. Int4 offers compression but at the cost of meaningful hallucination drift for certain slices and should not be auto-enabled for customer-facing routes. The gating thresholds above are conservative but actionable; they map directly into the onboarding CI and per-route rollout policies in the console.

Next steps (owners):
- Priya: open the quant-aware fine-tune pilot for int4 (due 2025-02-14).
- Ethan: add slice-level monitors and alerts to the console (jira JIRA-ML-2013).
- Sofia: coordinate 2-week internal canary for AWQ on hosted with fp16 fallback test (start 2025-02-10).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc purposely focuses on a compact slice taxonomy and three composite metrics to make tradeoffs actionable. Please flag if any slice definition should be split further for your product area.
